title: Tamsin and the Extraction
premise: Zephyrine Amberdale, interpreter for the faltering Meridian Accords delegation, witnesses a diplomatic flight erased from every radar, manifest, and memory mid-air—aboard it, the one witness who could expose a trilateral conspiracy to manufacture war. Branded a liability and hunted by an assassin embedded in their own security detail, Zephyrine must smuggle the flight's black-box transcript across three hostile jurisdictions with only a forged passport and a translator's ear for lies. The extraction succeeds at devastating cost: the truth surfaces, but Zephyrine must choose between the loyalty of the person who saved them and exposing that same person as the conspiracy's architect.
about_author: Wren Ishikawa is a former conference interpreter who spent a decade in rooms where wars were almost started by mistranslation. They write thrillers about people whose professions make them professionally invisible.

chapters.title: The Packed Bag
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. We meet them mid-negotiation in Vhalta City, interpreting a doomed peace session while mentally rehearsing escape routes. Their go-bag sits under the hotel bed; their polished lie—a fabricated nationality—sits under their tongue. Emotional beat: controlled dread, the exhaustion of permanent readiness.

chapters.title: Flight 114
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Aboard the delegation's charter, Zephyrine interprets a private exchange between envoy Casimir Renholt and a foreign minister that hints at sabotage of the accords. The plane shudders through unexplained turbulence; comms die for ninety seconds. Beat: unease sharpening into suspicion.

chapters.title: Erased
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, landing. Flight 114 never existed: no manifest, no tower log, no passengers on any list—including Zephyrine. Hotel key cards voided, colleagues staring through them. Only Renholt, alive and unbothered, acknowledges them. Beat: vertigo of unpersoning.

chapters.title: The Man Who Remembers
chapters.summary: Zephyrine confronts Renholt, who slips them a microcassette—the cockpit recording—and a warning: 'Someone bought the sky.' Security chief Davor Kestrel watches too closely. Beat: reluctant alliance, first taste of conspiracy's scale.

chapters.title: Kestrel
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV, revealed to readers but not Zephyrine: he is the assassin, tasked with recovering the cassette and closing accounts. His professionalism is chillingly domestic—he waters a plant, then reviews kill routes. Beat: dramatic irony, dread installed early.

chapters.title: Interpreter's Ear
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Listening to the tape, they catch what machines missed: a code phrase in the minister's accent-shifted speech confirming the crash was scheduled, not accidental. They memorize rather than carry it. Beat: competence as survival, quiet triumph.

chapters.title: First Blood
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Kestrel stages an 'evacuation' that is really an ambush; Zephyrine escapes through the hotel's service tunnels using a route from their go-bag planning. Renholt is taken. Beat: terror, the lie of safety collapsing.

chapters.title: Border of Paper
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Using forged papers and a border guard's boredom, they cross into Ostrava Province. Flashbacks reveal how they built their false identity—layer by layer, like translation. Beat: identity as craft, loneliness deepening.

chapters.title: The Archivist
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. In Ostrava they find Ilse Marchetti, a disgraced aviation registrar who keeps paper copies of everything digital. She confirms Flight 114 existed—and that its deletion order came from inside all three governments simultaneously. Beat: hope with teeth.

chapters.title: Three Signatures
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV. She explains the mechanism: a trilateral 'continuity protocol' letting each government erase events jointly—designed for disasters, repurposed for murder. The accords' failure would justify emergency powers everywhere. Beat: theme crystallized—power corrupting its own safeguards.

chapters.title: What Kestrel Keeps
chapters.summary: Kestrel's POV. He interrogates Renholt, learning Zephyrine has the transcript memorized—not written. His handlers order Zephyrine's death 'quietly,' but Kestrel hesitates: Zephyrine is the first target who listened back. Beat: assassin's doubt, humanity flickering.

chapters.title: Safehouse Sonata
chapters.summary: Zephyrine and Ilse hide in a shuttered concert hall. Zephyrine recites the transcript aloud to test their memory against Ilse's copy; a wrong word nearly gets them killed when a listening device betrays them. Beat: intimacy and paranoia entwined.

chapters.title: Ilse's Price
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Ilse demands publication credit and protection in exchange for going public—but Zephyrine realizes Ilse once sold data to the very protocol she now condemns. Loyalty vs. truth sharpens into personal betrayal. Beat: disillusionment.

chapters.title: The Long Train
chapters.summary: Split POV. Zephyrine rides a night train toward the neutral city of Corvane, sensing Kestrel aboard. A cat-and-mouse sequence through carriages ends in a truce at knifepoint: Kestrel wants out of the contract; his employers want him dead too. Beat: enemies becoming uneasy mirrors.

chapters.title: Corvane
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Neutral ground, press corps, one chance to broadcast. But the network editor who agrees to air the transcript is photographed meeting Renholt—released, and now visibly running the cover-up. Beat: trap disguised as rescue.

chapters.title: Broadcast Interrupted
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Live transmission begins; power dies at minute four. Kestrel pulls Zephyrine out through the studio's rigging, taking a bullet meant for them. Beat: betrayal confirmed, loyalty inverted—the assassin becomes the shield.

chapters.title: Renholt's Confession
chapters.summary: Renholt's POV. He engineered the erasure to force the accords' collapse, believing manufactured crisis preferable to real war later. He offers Zephyrine partnership: bury the truth, shape the peace. Beat: seduction of power, temptation articulated.

chapters.title: The Choice
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. With Kestrel wounded and Ilse's copy compromised, Zephyrine holds the truth only in memory. Renholt offers safety, legitimacy, an end to running—if they stay silent. Beat: the novel's thematic fulcrum, held breath.

chapters.title: Interpreted Live
chapters.summary: Climax, Zephyrine's POV. At the accords' final signing ceremony, Zephyrine walks in as 'staff,' takes the interpreter's booth, and renders Renholt's closing speech into three languages—inserting, word by word, the confession from Flight 114, live to every delegate. Beat: weaponized profession, triumphant audacity.

chapters.title: Consequences
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. Renholt arrested mid-ceremony; delegations fracture; Kestrel, bleeding, walks out past guards who've stopped caring. Ilse publishes her archive, claiming sole credit. Zephyrine's false identity unravels publicly. Beat: victory that costs every disguise.

chapters.title: What Survives Translation
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV. Testifying before a tribunal, Zephyrine must decide whether to name Kestrel as the assassin or let his file stay clean—he saved them, and he killed for the same machine. They tell the truth selectively: loyalty and truth negotiated, not chosen. Beat: moral complexity honored.

chapters.title: The Unpacked Bag
chapters.summary: Zephyrine's POV, epilogue. Months later, in a new city under their own name for the first time, Zephyrine unpacks the go-bag at last—keeps the cassette, donates the rest. A letter arrives from Kestrel: two words, 'Still listening.' Beat: earned peace, vigilance transformed into choice.
